subject: Archaeology
title: China's Terracotta Army
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: China's Terracotta Army.

hook.text: In 1974, Chinese farmers digging a well struck something hard. It was the head of a clay soldier.

buildup.text: They had stumbled onto the tomb guard of Emperor Qin Shi Huang, China's first emperor.

discovery.text: Over 8,000 life-sized soldiers were buried in formation, each with a unique face and hairstyle.

twist.text: The figures were originally painted in bright colors, but the paint dissolved within minutes of exposure to air.

climax.text: The emperor's actual tomb remains sealed. Scientists detected rivers of liquid mercury inside.

punchline.text: An army built to guard a tomb has become China's greatest tourist attraction.

quiz.question: What happened to the Terracotta Army's original paint?
options: It was carefully preserved by archaeologists
It dissolved within minutes of being exposed to air
It was removed by grave robbers centuries ago

details.summary: In 1974, farmers digging a well near Xi'an, China, uncovered the first of an estimated 8,000 life-sized terracotta warriors guarding the tomb of Emperor Qin Shi Huang. Each figure has unique facial features, and the tomb complex covers an area larger than some ancient cities.
details.whyItMatters: The Terracotta Army reveals the scale of power and labor that the first emperor of unified China commanded. It represents one of the most ambitious burial projects in human history and is still being excavated decades later.
takeaways: Discovered accidentally by farmers near Xi'an in 1974
An estimated 8,000 life-sized warriors with unique faces
Guards the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, first emperor of unified China

faq.question: Why does each terracotta warrior have a unique face?
faq.answer: Workers assembled warriors from standardized body parts but individualized the heads with different hairstyles, facial features, and expressions. This may reflect the actual soldiers of Qin's army. The combination of mass production and individual craftsmanship is remarkable for 200 BCE.

faq.question: Has the emperor's actual tomb been opened?
faq.answer: No. The burial mound itself has not been excavated. Ancient texts describe rivers of mercury inside, and modern soil testing has confirmed exceptionally high mercury levels in the mound. Chinese authorities are waiting for conservation technology advanced enough to protect whatever lies within.
